Research Query: What are the key principles of accessible UI design?

Please work together to answer this query comprehensively:
1. Planner: Create a research plan
2. Researcher: Gather evidence from web and academic sources
3. Writer: Synthesize findings into a well-cited response
4. Critic: Evaluate the quality and provide feedback

1) Planner — Research plan (step-by-step)
1.1 Define the key concepts to investigate
  - Core accessibility principles (high-level): e.g., POUR (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust)
  - Concrete design requirements and patterns (color contrast, keyboard access, labels, semantics, focus management, touch targets, captions)
  - Platform guidance and conventions (web WCAG, Apple HIG, Material, Microsoft Inclusive Design)
  - Testing & evaluation methods (automated tools, manual review, assistive-technology testing, user testing)
  - Legal/standards context and business/UX rationale (WCAG, Section 508, ADA, empirical evidence/on usability)
  - Gaps, trade-offs, and guidance for teams (prioritization, workflows)

1.2 Types of sources to collect
  - Standards and guidance: W3C/WAI (WCAG 2.1/2.2, ARIA), ISO where relevant
  - Platform vendor guidance: Apple HIG, Android/Material, Microsoft Inclusive Design
  - Practitioner resources and audits: WebAIM, Deque, Google Lighthouse docs, axe docs
  - UX research and academic studies: textbooks and peer-reviewed papers on accessibility/usability (Lazar, Horton, Quesenbery, Nielsen Norman Group)
  - Empirical scans / surveys: WebAIM Million, WebAIM Screen Reader Survey, accessibility audit reports
  - Legal/regulatory summaries: Section 508, ADA summaries, EN 301 549

1.3 Specific search queries to run
  - "WCAG principles POUR summary"
  - "key principles of accessible UI design"
  - "perceivable operable understandable robust examples"
  - "color contrast WCAG 2.1 4.5:1 large text 3:1"
  - "keyboard accessibility guidelines web forms focus order"
  - "ARIA best practices modals focus management"
  - "WebAIM screen reader survey 2020 results"
  - "WebAIM Million accessibility errors 2021"
  - "accessibility testing tools axe Lighthouse WAVE"
  - "inclusive design principles Microsoft Apple HIG accessibility"
  - "benefits of accessibility usability studies"
  - "accessibility guidelines mobile touch target size"
  - "legal requirements web accessibility ADA Section 508 WCAG"

1.4 How to synthesize findings
  - Map high-level principles (POUR + inclusive design) to concrete, actionable design rules.
  - For each principle provide: short definition, why it matters (including evidence/UX impact), specific implementation guidance (examples, numeric thresholds where applicable), and testing checks.
  - Provide prioritized checklist for designers and engineers (must-fix vs recommended).
  - Note platform differences (web vs native iOS/Android) and reference authoritative sources for each guideline.
  - List recommended tools and a testing workflow (automated -> manual -> assistive tech -> user testing).
  - Identify gaps and limitations in evidence and recommend next steps (e.g., research needed, accessibility user testing).

2) Researcher — Evidence and source summaries (web + academic)
Below are authoritative sources and short summaries of their relevant findings. (URLs given for direct reference.)

2.1 Standards & core principles
  - WCAG 2.1 & 2.2 (W3C WAI): Defines POUR (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and success criteria with testable requirements (contrast ratios, keyboard support, captions, resize text, focus visibility, etc.). Use as the primary checklist for web content accessibility. (W3C WCAG 2.1: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/ ; WCAG 2.2: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
  - WAI Introduction to Web Accessibility: Explains why accessibility matters and links to practices and resources. (https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro)

2.2 Platform & design guidance
  - Apple Human Interface Guidelines — Accessibility: Platform-specific guidance: VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, focus/labels, accessibility traits. (https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility/overview/)
  - Material Design — Accessibility: Contrast, touch target sizes, focus states, text scaling, semantics for Android. (https://material.io/design/usability/accessibility.html)
  - Microsoft Inclusive Design & accessibility docs: Inclusive design principles and practical guidance for Windows apps and cross-platform products. (https://www.microsoft.com/design/inclusive)

2.3 Practitioner resources & audits
  - WebAIM: WebAIM Million (site scan of top 1M homepages) — shows the most common WCAG failures (missing alt text, low contrast, empty links). Useful for prioritizing common fixes. (https://webaim.org/projects/million/)
  - WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey — reports on assistive tech usage patterns and common pain points; reinforces importance of semantics, keyboard access, and clear labels. (https://webaim.org/projects/screenreadersurvey6/)
  - Deque Systems / axe docs: practical guidance and automated rules; good resource for developers to interpret WCAG into code checks. (https://www.deque.com/axe/)

2.4 UX and research literature
  - "A Web for Everyone" — Horton & Quesenbery (2014): practical, research-informed guidance on inclusive web design; emphasizes designing for multiple needs and contexts.
  - Nielsen Norman Group articles on accessibility/usability: show that accessibility improvements often improve overall usability; provide examples and research-backed heuristics for inclusive UI. (e.g., https://www.nngroup.com/articles/accessibility-usability/)
  - Jonathan Lazar et al., "Ensuring Digital Accessibility through Process and Policy" (book): covers process-level integration of accessibility into software development and empirical evidence for accessibility practices.

2.5 Testing tools & methods
  - Google Lighthouse (Accessibility audits) — automated checks in Chrome DevTools. (https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse/audits/accessibility)
  - Accessibility evaluation tools: WAVE (WebAIM), axe (Deque), Color Contrast Analyzer — used for automated checks and spotting common issues.
  - Screen readers: NVDA (Windows), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS), TalkBack (Android) — manual testing with these is critical.
  - Testing workflow best practice: automated scanning -> manual code review -> keyboard-only testing -> screen reader testing -> user testing with people with disabilities (recommended by WAI and practitioners).

2.6 Legal & standards context
  - Section 508 (US federal accessibility standard) and ADA interpretations: legal drivers for accessibility; WCAG is commonly used as the technical standard. (https://www.section508.gov/)
  - EN 301 549 (EU): procurement standard mapping to WCAG.

3) Writer — Synthesized, actionable summary of the key principles of accessible UI design (with citations)
Below is a concise, actionable synthesis that maps principles to concrete design rules and test checks.

3.1 High-level principles (what to design for)
  1) Perceivable — Make content available to the senses used by people to access it.
     - What it means: Provide text alternatives (alt text), captions/transcripts for audio/video, sufficient color contrast, and ensure content is not delivered only via color, sound, or visual-only cues.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Provide alt text or meaningful null alt for images (WCAG).
       - Captions for prerecorded video; live captions where possible (WCAG).
       - Contrast ratios: at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (WCAG) — check with Color Contrast Analyzer or automated tools.
       - Do not rely on color alone to convey meaning (e.g., error fields).
     - Test checks: automated contrast checker, manual review of images for alt text, captions present for media. (W3C WCAG)

  2) Operable — Ensure users can operate UI with their available input methods.
     - What it means: Keyboard accessibility, sufficient time to act, predictable focus, and avoidance of traps.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - All interactive elements must be reachable and usable with keyboard alone (tab, enter, space, arrow keys where appropriate).
       - Visible focus indicators that are not removed.
       - Logical and predictable tab order; provide skip links for long pages.
       - Don’t use very short time limits without a way to extend them.
       - For touch: sufficiently large touch targets (Material recommends 48 dp; Apple recommends ~44pt).
     - Test checks: keyboard-only walkthrough, focus visibility checks, mobile touch target measurements. (W3C WCAG; Apple HIG; Material)

  3) Understandable — Make content and the operation of the UI clear.
     - What it means: Clear language, consistent UI, helpful labels and instructions, meaningful error messages and recovery.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Use clear, concise labels for controls; avoid ambiguous icons without labels.
       - Provide inline validation with clear instructions and suggestions for correction.
       - Use predictable navigation and consistent layouts.
       - Allow users to pause/mute moving content or animations that distract.
     - Test checks: readability checks, consistency review, review of form validation wording and guidance. (W3C WCAG)

  4) Robust — Ensure content works with current and future assistive technologies.
     - What it means: Use semantic markup, expose UI semantics correctly (ARIA only when necessary), and follow platform accessibility APIs.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Use native HTML elements where possible (button, input, select) so browsers and AT understand behavior.
       - When using ARIA, follow WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices to expose roles, states, and properties correctly.
       - Test across browsers and assistive tech (NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack).
     - Test checks: semantic HTML audit, ARIA validation, assistive-technology testing. (W3C ARIA; W3C WCAG)

3.2 Cross-cutting design principles and patterns
  - Provide alternatives and redundancy: combine visual, text, and audio cues where appropriate.
  - Progressive enhancement and graceful degradation: content should be available even if advanced features fail.
  - Minimize cognitive load: simple language, grouping related fields, clear affordances.
  - Consistency and predictability: consistent layouts and interaction patterns reduce error rates.
  - Respect user preferences: support text resizing, reduced-motion preferences (prefers-reduced-motion), high-contrast modes.
  - Inclusive interaction design: consider low vision, motor, cognitive, auditory, and temporary situational impairments.

3.3 Concrete implementation checklist (prioritized)
  Must-have (first pass)
    - Ensure keyboard access for all interactive elements (tab order, Enter/Space activation).
    - Provide meaningful alt text for images; decorative images use empty alt.
    - Ensure sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 normal text).
    - Use semantic HTML/controls and correct ARIA roles if needed.
    - Provide visible focus indicators and skip links for long pages.
    - Add captions/transcripts for video and descriptive labels for audio.
  Recommended (next pass)
    - Review forms: labels associated with inputs, clear error messages, instructions.
    - Ensure responsive spacing, adequate touch target sizes.
    - Implement prefers-reduced-motion support, and respect OS-level text scaling.
    - Add landmarks and heading structure for navigation.
  Ongoing/process
    - Add accessibility checks to CI (axe, Lighthouse).
    - Manual accessibility testing (keyboard + screen readers).
    - Include people with disabilities in usability testing.

3.4 Testing workflow & tools
  - Automated checks (fast, catch common issues): axe, Lighthouse, WAVE (Deque/WebAIM).
  - Manual code review and semantic checks: ensure proper use of elements and ARIA.
  - Interaction testing:
    - Keyboard-only navigation walkthrough.
    - Screen reader testing (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, TalkBack on Android).
    - Mobile testing (touch targets, orientation, gestures).
  - User testing: recruit participants with a range of abilities for realistic validation (recommended by WAI and accessibility practitioners).
  - Recommended tools: axe (Deque), Lighthouse (Chrome), WAVE (WebAIM), Color Contrast Analyzer, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack. (Sources: Deque, Google, WebAIM, W3C)

3.5 Why accessibility matters (evidence & ROI)
  - Legal/compliance: Many jurisdictions require accessible digital services (WCAG commonly used as technical standard; see Section 508, ADA).
  - Usability improvements: Accessibility practices often improve overall UX (NN/g, WAI).
  - Business reach: Accessible products reach more users, reduce support costs, and improve SEO and mobile friendliness.
  - Empirical observations: Large scans (WebAIM Million) show common, fixable issues that significantly impact many users.

Key citations:
  - W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 & 2.2 — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/ ; https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
  - W3C WAI introductions & ARIA practices — https://www.w3.org/WAI/ ; https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-practices/
  - WebAIM — WebAIM Million and Screen Reader Survey — https://webaim.org/projects/million/ ; https://webaim.org/projects/screenreadersurvey6/
  - Deque / axe — https://www.deque.com/axe/
  - Google Lighthouse accessibility audits — https://developers.google.com/web/tools/lighthouse/audits
  - Apple HIG Accessibility — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility/overview/
  - Material Design accessibility — https://material.io/design/usability/accessibility.html
  - NN/g articles on accessibility & usability — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/accessibility-usability/
  - Horton & Quesenbery, A Web for Everyone (book)
  - Microsoft Inclusive Design — https://www.microsoft.com/design/inclusive

4) Critic — Quality evaluation, limitations, and next steps
4.1 Strengths of the research and synthesis
  - Grounded in authoritative standards (WCAG/WAI) and platform guidance (Apple, Material, Microsoft).
  - Uses practitioner evidence (WebAIM, Deque) to prioritize common, high-impact fixes.
  - Produces actionable rules with measurable thresholds (contrast ratios, keyboard checks, touch sizes).
  - Provides a testing workflow that combines automated and manual testing plus user testing.

4.2 Limitations and gaps
  - Web-centric emphasis: WCAG focus means native app nuances may need platform-specific deep dives (iOS/Android nuances are summarized but not exhaustive).
  - Academic empirical research: while practitioner reports and standards are strong, high-quality peer-reviewed studies quantifying the UX gains from specific accessibility fixes are fewer and more fragmented; more controlled experiments would strengthen evidence about which fixes yield the largest usability gains for particular user groups.
  - Cognitive accessibility: guidance on cognitive and learning disabilities is less prescriptive in WCAG; designers should consult specialized research and involve users with cognitive disabilities in testing.
  - International legal variability: summarized legal context is high-level; teams should consult legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific obligations.

4.3 Recommendations for further work
  - Run an accessibility audit of your product (automated + manual + screen reader + keyboard).
  - Conduct user testing with people who have a range of disabilities to validate assumptions and discover real-world issues.
  - Integrate accessibility into design and development workflows: design tokens for contrast, component library with accessible patterns, CI checks.
  - Keep up with evolving standards (WCAG updates, platform accessibility changes) and iterative accessibility regression testing.

If you want, I can now:
  - Produce a one-page prioritized accessibility checklist tailored to web or mobile,
  - Generate example code snippets (semantic HTML + ARIA patterns) for common components (modal, form, nav),
  - Or run through a step-by-step test plan you can use with your product. Which would help you most next?

This response brings together a research plan, evidence summary, an actionable synthesis of the key principles of accessible UI design, and a short critique of the findings. The synthesis maps high‑level accessibility principles to concrete design rules, testing checks, platforms, and tools so designers and engineers can apply them directly.

1) Planner — Research plan (summary)
- Key concepts to investigate: core principles (POUR), concrete UI patterns (contrast, keyboard, semantics, focus, touch targets, captions), platform guidance (WCAG, Apple HIG, Material, Microsoft), testing methods (automated + manual + assistive technology + user testing), legal context (WCAG, Section 508, ADA), and team workflows/prioritization.

2) Researcher — Evidence summary (key sources and takeaways)
- WCAG 2.1 / 2.2 (W3C WAI): Establishes the POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and concrete, testable success criteria (e.g., contrast ratios, keyboard support, captions, resize text) that are widely used as the technical standard for web accessibility [Source: W3C — WCAG 2.1/2.2].
- WAI ARIA Authoring Practices: Guidance on when and how to use ARIA roles, states, and properties to expose semantics to assistive technologies; emphasizes using native elements first [Source: W3C — WAI-ARIA Practices].
- Apple Human Interface Guidelines — Accessibility: Platform guidance for VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, accessibility labels/traits, and platform‑specific patterns [Source: Apple — Human Interface Guidelines: Accessibility].
- Material Design — Accessibility: Guidance for Android and cross‑platform apps (touch target sizes, contrast, text scaling, focus states) and examples of accessible components [Source: Material Design — Accessibility].
- Microsoft / Inclusive Design: Principles and practices to design for a broad range of abilities and contexts; practical patterns and research rationale [Source: Microsoft — Inclusive Design].
- WebAIM (WebAIM Million; Screen Reader Survey): Empirical findings about the most common accessibility defects (missing alt text, low contrast, empty links) and assistive‑technology usage/pain points — useful for prioritizing fixes [Source: WebAIM — WebAIM Million; WebAIM — Screen Reader Survey].
- Deque / axe & Google Lighthouse: Practitioner tooling and rulesets that map WCAG criteria to automated checks; used in CI and developer workflows [Source: Deque — axe; Google — Lighthouse].
- Nielsen Norman Group and Horton & Quesenbery (“A Web for Everyone”): Evidence and arguments that accessibility improvements often improve overall usability and user satisfaction; practical design guidance for inclusive interfaces [Source: Nielsen Norman Group; Horton & Quesenbery — A Web for Everyone].

3) Writer — Synthesized principles, rules, and checklist

A. High‑level principles (POUR) and what to do
- Perceivable — Make content available to the senses used to access it.
  - Why: If users cannot perceive content (e.g., low contrast, no captions), they cannot use it.
  - Concrete rules:
    - Text contrast: ≥4.5:1 for normal text, ≥3:1 for large text; check with color contrast tools [Source: W3C — WCAG].
    - Provide alt text for meaningful images; use empty alt for decorative images [Source: W3C — WCAG; WebAIM].
    - Provide captions/transcripts for prerecorded video; caption/live caption where feasible [Source: W3C — WCAG].
    - Avoid conveying information by color alone; include text or icons as redundant cues [Source: W3C — WCAG].
  - Tests: Color contrast analyzer, manual alt‑text review, media checks for captions.

- Operable — Ensure UI can be operated with available input methods.
  - Why: Users with mobility or input limitations may use keyboard, switch devices, or assistive tech.
  - Concrete rules:
    - All interactive controls operable by keyboard (tab order, Enter/Space activation; arrow keys where appropriate) [Source: W3C — WCAG].
    - Visible focus indicators (do not remove default outlines without an accessible replacement).
    - Logical focus order and skip links for long pages.
    - Provide adequate time or ability to extend time limits.
    - Touch targets: ~44 pt / 48 dp recommended minimum for mobile targets (platform guidance) [Source: Apple HIG; Material Design].
  - Tests: Keyboard-only navigation, focus visibility review, mobile touch measurement.

- Understandable — Make UI behavior and content clear.
  - Why: Cognitive clarity reduces errors and supports comprehension.
  - Concrete rules:
    - Use clear labels and instructions for form fields and controls; associate labels with inputs.
    - Provide helpful, actionable error messages and inline validation.
    - Maintain consistent navigation, predictable behavior, and avoid surprising interactions.
    - Respect user preferences (text scaling, reduced motion).
  - Tests: Readability checks, review of form error messages, consistency audit.

- Robust — Ensure content works with assistive technologies now and in the future.
  - Why: Semantics and stable APIs let AT interpret UI correctly.
  - Concrete rules:
    - Use native semantic elements when possible (button, input, heading levels).
    - When using ARIA, follow WAI‑ARIA authoring practices; don’t duplicate native semantics.
    - Test across screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack) and browsers.
  - Tests: Semantic HTML audit, ARIA correctness review, assistive‑tech testing [Source: W3C ARIA; WebAIM; Deque].

B. Cross‑cutting design patterns
- Provide redundancy of cues (visual + text + audio where relevant).
- Minimize cognitive load: group related fields, reduce unnecessary steps, avoid ambiguous icons.
- Progressive enhancement: ensure core content accessible without advanced scripting.
- Design for flexibly scaled text and varying contrast environments.

C. Prioritized implementation checklist
Must‑fix (first pass)
  - Keyboard access for all interactive elements.
  - Meaningful alt text or empty alt for decorations.
  - Sufficient contrast for text and UI components.
  - Visible focus indicators; skip links for content‑heavy pages.
  - Captions/transcripts for media.
Recommended (next)
  - Proper labels linked to inputs; clear error handling.
  - Touch target sizes and spacing on mobile.
  - Respect prefers‑reduced‑motion and text scaling.
  - Landmarks and heading structure for navigation.
Ongoing process
  - Integrate automated checks (axe, Lighthouse) into CI.
  - Manual keyboard and screen reader testing.
  - Regular user testing including people with disabilities.

D. Testing workflow and tools

2.1 Standards & core principles

Use as the primary checklist for web content accessibility. (W3C WCAG 2.1: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/ ; WCAG 2.2: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)

  - WebAIM: WebAIM Million (site scan of top 1M homepages) — shows the most common WCAG failures (missing alt text, low contrast, empty links). Useful for prioritizing common fixes. (https://webaim.org/projects/million/)

  - "A Web for Everyone" — Horton & Quesenbery (2014): practical, research-informed guidance on inclusive web design; emphasizes designing for multiple needs and contexts.

3) Writer — Synthesized, actionable summary of the key principles of accessible UI design (with citations)
Below is a concise, actionable synthesis that maps principles to concrete design rules and test checks.

3.1 High-level principles (what to design for)
  1) Perceivable — Make content available to the senses used by people to access it.
     - What it means: Provide text alternatives (alt text), captions/transcripts for audio/video, sufficient color contrast, and ensure content is not delivered only via color, sound, or visual-only cues.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Provide alt text or meaningful null alt for images (WCAG).
       - Captions for prerecorded video; live captions where possible (WCAG).
       - Contrast ratios: at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (WCAG) — check with Color Contrast Analyzer or automated tools.
       - Do not rely on color alone to convey meaning (e.g., error fields).
     - Test checks: automated contrast checker, manual review of images for alt text, captions present for media. (W3C WCAG)

  2) Operable — Ensure users can operate UI with their available input methods.
     - What it means: Keyboard accessibility, sufficient time to act, predictable focus, and avoidance of traps.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - All interactive elements must be reachable and usable with keyboard alone (tab, enter, space, arrow keys where appropriate).
       - Visible focus indicators that are not removed.
       - Logical and predictable tab order; provide skip links for long pages.
       - Don’t use very short time limits without a way to extend them.
       - For touch: sufficiently large touch targets (Material recommends 48 dp; Apple recommends ~44pt).
     - Test checks: keyboard-only walkthrough, focus visibility checks, mobile touch target measurements. (W3C WCAG; Apple HIG; Material)

  3) Understandable — Make content and the operation of the UI clear.
     - What it means: Clear language, consistent UI, helpful labels and instructions, meaningful error messages and recovery.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Use clear, concise labels for controls; avoid ambiguous icons without labels.
       - Provide inline validation with clear instructions and suggestions for correction.
       - Use predictable navigation and consistent layouts.
       - Allow users to pause/mute moving content or animations that distract.
     - Test checks: readability checks, consistency review, review of form validation wording and guidance. (W3C WCAG)

  4) Robust — Ensure content works with current and future assistive technologies.
     - What it means: Use semantic markup, expose UI semantics correctly (ARIA only when necessary), and follow platform accessibility APIs.
     - Concrete rules/examples:
       - Use native HTML elements where possible (button, input, select) so browsers and AT understand behavior.
       - When using ARIA, follow WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices to expose roles, states, and properties correctly.
       - Test across browsers and assistive tech (NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack).
     - Test checks: semantic HTML audit, ARIA validation, assistive-technology testing. (W3C ARIA; W3C WCAG)

3.2 Cross-cutting design principles and patterns
  - Provide alternatives and redundancy: combine visual, text, and audio cues where appropriate.
  - Progressive enhancement and graceful degradation: content should be available even if advanced features fail.
  - Minimize cognitive load: simple language, grouping related fields, clear affordances.
  - Consistency and predictability: consistent layouts and interaction patterns reduce error rates.
  - Respect user preferences: support text resizing, reduced-motion preferences (prefers-reduced-motion), high-contrast modes.
  - Inclusive interaction design: consider low vision, motor, cognitive, auditory, and temporary situational impairments.

3.3 Concrete implementation checklist (prioritized)

    - Ensure keyboard access for all interactive elements (tab order, Enter/Space activation).
    - Provide meaningful alt text for images; decorative images use empty alt.
    - Ensure sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 normal text).
    - Use semantic HTML/controls and correct ARIA roles if needed.
    - Provide visible focus indicators and skip links for long pages.
    - Add captions/transcripts for video and descriptive labels for audio.
  Recommended (next pass)
    - Review forms: labels associated with inputs, clear error messages, instructions.
    - Ensure responsive spacing, adequate touch target sizes.
    - Implement prefers-reduced-motion support, and respect OS-level text scaling.
    - Add landmarks and heading structure for navigation.
  Ongoing/process
    - Add accessibility checks to CI (axe, Lighthouse).
    - Manual accessibility testing (keyboard + screen readers).
    - Include people with disabilities in usability testing.

3.4 Testing workflow & tools
  - Automated checks (fast, catch common issues): axe, Lighthouse, WAVE (Deque/WebAIM).
  - Manual code review and semantic checks: ensure proper use of elements and ARIA.
  - Interaction testing:
    - Keyboard-only navigation walkthrough.
    - Screen reader testing (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, TalkBack on Android).
    - Mobile testing (touch targets, orientation, gestures).
  - User testing: recruit participants with a range of abilities for realistic validation (recommended by WAI and accessibility practitioners).
  - Recommended tools: axe (Deque), Lighthouse (Chrome), WAVE (WebAIM), Color Contrast Analyzer, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack. (Sources: Deque, Google, WebAIM, W3C)

  - Legal/compliance: Many jurisdictions require accessible digital services (WCAG commonly used as technical standard; see Section 508, ADA).
  - Usability improvements: Accessibility practices often improve overall UX (NN/g, WAI).
  - Business reach: Accessible products reach more users, reduce support costs, and improve SEO and mobile friendliness.
  - Empirical observations: Large scans (WebAIM Million) show common, fixable issues that significantly impact many users.

metadata.critique:
Evaluation summary (criteria: Relevance, Evidence Quality, Completeness, Accuracy, Clarity)

Overall judgment: The Option B plan and writer draft are well structured and largely correct. They address the original query and the Critic’s prior requests, and they propose a practical, reproducible deliverable set. However, the deliverable is not yet fully defensible because several high‑priority items remain unimplemented (live provenance with access dates; exact WCAG SC quotes inserted; peer‑reviewed citations; validated runnable CI and test outputs; and a few expanded technical precisions). Before I could approve, the team must complete those items and tighten a few accuracy and completeness points listed below.

Detailed feedback and required improvements (prioritized)

1) Provenance / search log (must fix)
- Problem: The provenance-template.csv is fine as a template, but the final deliverable must include a populated provenance.csv with timestamps and the top‑3 results for every query. The Critic explicitly required no “No search results found” placeholders.
- Action: Run the exact queries from the template (or enable browsing to let the researcher do so), and populate provenance.csv with:
  - engine/database used, UTC timestamp, top 3 result titles + URLs per query.
  - For each WCAG SC used, include the exact SC page URL and the date accessed.
- Why: This is required for defensibility and reviewer verification.

2) Exact WCAG Success Criterion citations & quotes (must fix)
- Problem: Many normative claims cite WCAG by number; the deliverable must include the exact SC title, level (A/AA/AAA), and 1–2 sentence quoted excerpt (or exact wording) immediately adjacent to each rule that depends on it.
- Action: For each claim (contrast thresholds, large‑text definition, keyboard, captions, non‑text contrast, error handling, etc.), insert the SC number, SC title, WCAG level, the short quote, and the SC URL (from the populated provenance log).
- Why: Avoids paraphrase drift and ensures legal/technical traceability.

3) Peer‑reviewed empirical evidence (high priority)
- Problem: The plan acknowledges limited academic retrieval. The final deliverable must either include 2–3 peer‑reviewed papers (with full citations, DOIs/URLs, short summaries of methods/results) or explicitly state why such papers were unavailable and provide exact scholar queries.
- Action: Run the scholar queries, capture 2–3 suitable empirical studies (CHI/ASSETS/TOCHI or HCI journals) that support claims about usability/ROI or assistive-tech usage; add concise summaries (methods, N, outcomes) and cite DOIs.
- Why: Strengthens the evidence base and answers the Critic’s request.

4) Runnable CI examples (must fix)
- Problem: Pseudo snippets are useful but reviewers expect copy‑paste runnable GitHub Actions YAML that is syntactically correct and references real actions/repos.
- Action:
  - Provide a tested dequelabs/axe-action YAML and a tested lighthouse-ci Action YAML with example configuration for (a) local dev server and (b) deployed preview URL. Include notes on required secrets/ports and how to interpret results.
  - Include examples of threshold checks: e.g., fail PR if axe violations > 0 or accessibility score < 90, and show how violations are reported (artifact/PR comment).
- Why: Enables teams to adopt CI quickly and validates the guidance.

5) Tested code examples + automation outputs (must fix)
- Problem: Code snippets are correct conceptually but must be run and validated. The Critic requires axe/Lighthouse outputs demonstrating the examples produce no high‑severity violations.
- Action:
  - Run the three example pages locally, execute axe‑core CLI and Lighthouse, save JSON outputs to test-results/, and include a 1‑page summary of results (violation counts and names). If any violations appear, fix examples until high‑impact issues are resolved.
  - Include the exact commands used and reference the results files in the deliverable.
- Why: Demonstrates that the code examples are production‑ready and confirms the guidance.

6) ARIA/modal/live‑region depth and pitfalls (high priority)
- Problem: Provide more explicit, tested guidance on:
  - Modal dialogs: inert vs aria-hidden, focus trapping, restoring focus, and recommended libraries (focus-trap, @reach/dialog, Radix). Note browser support for inert and link to polyfill.
  - ARIA pitfalls: at least 2 concrete before/after examples showing how misuse breaks AT (e.g., role=button on div without keyboard handlers; aria-hidden on interactive descendants) and explaining AT failure modes.
  - Live regions: when to use aria-live vs moving focus, politeness settings, and pitfalls such as update flooding.
- Action: Add tested modal implementation (using a recommended library + inert handling) and run AT checks (keyboard + screen reader verification recommended in appendix).
- Why: These are common failure modes causing serious accessibility regressions.

7) Forms and error summary (medium priority)
- Problem: Expand the form examples to include a standard error summary pattern (linked anchors to fields), ARIA attributes used (aria-describedby, aria-invalid), and handling of validation timing (inline vs on submit).
- Action: Add a minimal error summary pattern implementation, test with keyboard navigation and axe/Lighthouse, and include results.
- Why: Forms are frequent accessibility pain points—examples must be explicit.

8) Legal mapping and user‑testing protocol (medium priority)
- Problem: The legal appendix should include precise links and a brief mapping (e.g., Section 508 mapping to WCAG 2.0/2.1 / EN 301 549), and the user‑testing protocol should include recruitment, consent, sample-size guidance, tasks, and metrics.
- Action: Populate the legal mapping with authoritative URLs and a one‑paragraph advisory about consulting counsel. Expand the user testing appendix with recruitment sources and ethical considerations.
- Why: Completes compliance context and supports practical testing.

9) Deliverable hygiene and traceability (minor)
- Problem: Ensure no placeholders remain (e.g., “to verify” or “No search results”), add a changelog mapping Critic items to where they were addressed, and ensure every numeric claim is linked to a source.
- Action: Final QA pass: check provenance.csv is complete, writer.md contains direct SC quotes, checklist.pdf included, README explains how to run tests and CI.
- Why: Final reviewers will expect full traceability.

- One‑page checklist in Markdown and exported PDF, user‑testing protocol, legal mapping appendix, and changelog.

Conclusion / Next steps
The Option B artifacts proposed are on the right track. Implement the nine prioritized improvements above (start with populating the provenance log and inserting direct WCAG SC quotes), run the code validations, and incorporate the peer‑reviewed studies or the exact scholar query results.
